title: How Did the FBI Record Him Without Ever Touching the Phone Booth? #Shorts
description:
The FBI recorded every word he said in a glass phone booth — and never once opened the door. The Supreme Court still called it an illegal search.

In Los Angeles in the mid-1960s, agents taped a hidden microphone to the outside of a public phone booth that Charles Katz used to place illegal betting calls, and never set foot inside. For nearly forty years the rule had been simple: no physical trespass, no search. But Katz had shut the door to keep his words private.

In Katz v. United States (1967), the Court ruled seven to one that the Fourth Amendment "protects people, not places." Recording him without a warrant was unconstitutional — not because wiretapping is banned, but because it needed a judge's permission first. Justice Harlan's concurrence gave the "reasonable expectation of privacy" test that still governs surveillance today.

Watch the full story on the channel.
